newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU leaders set date for first meeting with Blair.
newsitem.headline: EU leaders set date for first meeting with Blair.

text.p: EU leaders will hold their first meeting with Tony Blair in three weeks time amid cautious optimism it will prove easier to do business with Britain's new Labour prime minister than with his Conservative predecessors.

Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, whose country currently holds the European Union presidency, said Blair and the 14 other EU leaders would meet for a brief, informal summit meeting in the Dutch seaside resort of Noordwijk on May 23.
The meeting has been called to keep the bloc on track for landmark reforms at a formal mid-June summit in Amsterdam and will be preceded by a meeting of EU foreign ministers on May 20.
Van Mierlo said the British people had voted overwhelmingly for change and that its European partners hoped to benefit from the feeling in Britain that new roads were opening up.
"Perhaps one of these roads leads a bit more directly to Europe," he told a news conference.
Van Mierlo said that while on some issues Labour was more in line with other EU members than the Conservatives, Britain's new government would still drive a hard bargain in other areas.
"I have no cheap illusions. I know very well that the difficulties have not all suddenly disappeared," he said.
Britons of the Right and the Left were all island dwellers and the country's insular character would continue to set its stamp on British attitudes to Europe, Van Mierlo added.
Van Mierlo said he assumed the new British government would be able to get down to business quickly, though it would first need to digest the election result.
However, the sheer scale of his victory gave Blair considerable room for maneouvre on European policy.
"There's an enormous majority for Tony Blair, so if he wants there is room in which we can perhaps find consensus on important questions...I'm optimistic," Van Mierlo said.
Van Mierlo said the Noordwijk summit would be "very informal" and would cover the key issues of the so-called inter-governmental conference (IGC).

This ongoing ministerial review of the EU's "constitution" aims to produce a more efficient and transparent Union, paving the way for an ambitious eastward expansion that could see up to a dozen ex-communist states joining in the next decade.
But, just six weeks before EU leaders are due to sign landmark treaty reforms at Amsterdam, negotiations are bogged down over the nuts and bolts of institutional change.
Sticking points include the future size of the European Commission and how to ensure the decision-making process fairly represents each country's population.
Van Mierlo said the extra summit would give member states the chance to quiz Blair on his stance towards deeper EU integration as planned under the IGC.
Blair's Labour Party, which won a resounding victory in Thursday's general election, is widely seen as more cooperative towards Europe than the defeated Conservatives.
